# The Asian Giant Softshell Turtle (*Pelochelys cantorii*)

![Asian Giant Softshell Turtle resting on a riverbed](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Pelochelys_cantorii.jpg/800px-Pelochelys_cantorii.jpg)
*An Asian Giant Softshell Turtle in its natural habitat*

The Asian giant softshell turtle (*Pelochelys cantorii*), also known as Cantor's giant softshell turtle, is one of the largest and most mysterious freshwater turtles in the world. This remarkable reptile can grow up to six feet in length and weigh over 200 pounds, making it a true giant among freshwater species (Stanford et al. 23). Its flat, olive-green body and smooth, leathery shell distinguish it from hard-shelled turtles, giving it a unique and almost alien appearance.

This species is found across Southeast Asia, including regions of India, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand, Malaysia, Vietnam, Cambodia, and the Philippines. It inhabits freshwater rivers, streams, and estuaries, preferring sandy or muddy substrates where it can bury itself and remain camouflaged (Das 112). The turtle spends an estimated 95% of its life buried motionless in sand or mud, surfacing only twice a day to breathe. It is an ambush predator, feeding primarily on fish, crustaceans, and mollusks by striking with remarkable speed when prey ventures too close (Bhupathy and Webb 45).

![Softshell turtle partially buried in sand](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/62/Pelochelys_bibroni.jpg/800px-Pelochelys_bibroni.jpg)
*A softshell turtle demonstrating its burrowing behavior*

Unfortunately, the Asian giant softshell turtle is currently listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List. Habitat destruction, pollution, sand mining, and hunting for its meat and eggs have drastically reduced its population across its range. In many areas, the species has become extremely rare or locally extinct (Stanford et al. 24). Conservation efforts, particularly in Cambodia and India, have focused on protecting nesting sites and raising awareness among local communities. Captive breeding programs have also been initiated to help bolster wild populations.

The Asian giant softshell turtle serves as an important reminder of the incredible biodiversity found in Asia's freshwater ecosystems and the urgent need to protect these vulnerable habitats before it is too late.

---

## Bibliography

Bhupathy, Subramanian, and Robert G. Webb. "In Search of Cantor's Giant Softshell Turtle." *Chelonian Conservation and Biology*, vol. 5, no. 1, 2004, pp. 40–49.

Das, Indraneil. *A Field Guide to the Reptiles of South-East Asia*. Bloomsbury Publishing, 2010.

Stanford, Craig B., et al. "Turtles and Tortoises Are in Trouble." *Current Biology*, vol. 30, no. 12, 2020, pp. R721–R735.
